optimal in the sense of (3). Hence, if the exact parameters

usual SPRT with these thresholds. For example, this can be
the case in settings where the (asymptotic) approximations
by Siegmund [5] are reliable (see Section VI for a more
detailed discussion of this approach). However, we will see
that our approach can be applied in a much broader range of
settings, including in some nonparametric settings (like testing
exchangeability using conformal martingales), and provides
non-asymptotic control of the type I and type II error. Further
advantages over Siegmund’s and other approaches, such as the
use of numerical methods to determine the exact thresholds,
are discussed in Section VI-B.

One line of work approximates the exact type I and type
II error of SPRTs based on Brownian motion and renewal
theory [5], [31], [32], [33]. This approach was particularly
driven by Siegmund, who gives a comprehensive overview in
his book [5]. The provided approximations are asymptotically
(for α →0 and β →0) correct under certain assumptions
including i.i.d. test statistics. Furthermore, using the Markov
property of the likelihood ratio in simple i.i.d. settings, one
can obtain the exact operating characteristics of the SPRT by
solving Fredholm integral equations (see, e.g., [34], [35], [36]).

it back into the expectation ((12) in the one-sided or (28)

be found. In this way, one can always ensure that the resulting
test is conservative, meaning that it provides the desired type
I and type II error. This is neither possible with Siegmund’s
approach nor when using simulations.

blocks.text: We introduced a general approach to uniformly improve

lines.text: We introduced a general approach to uniformly improve

spans.text: We introduced a general approach to uniformly improve

blocks.text:
nonnegative (super)martingale based sequential tests by avoid-
ing an overshoot at the upper threshold 1/α (where α is
the desired type I error). We illustrated its application by
uniformly improving the conservative power-one SPRT for
one-sided null and alternative hypotheses. We also obtained an
alternative to the two-sided SPRT with Wald’s approximated
thresholds, where our alternative provides valid type I and
type II error control while often reducing the sample size.
Our sequential tests can also be used to tighten conﬁdence
sequences and apply in nontrivial settings like sampling with-
out replacement and conformal martingales.

a cornerstone of sequential analysis. Based on desired type-I,
II error levels α, β, it stops when the likelihood ratio crosses
certain thresholds, guaranteeing optimality of the expected sam-
ple size. However, these thresholds are not closed form and the
test is often applied with approximate thresholds (1 −β)/α
and β/(1 −α) (approximate SPRT). When β

Wald’s approximated thresholds (4), then the SPRT stops for
rejection if Λt ≥1/α, but never stops for accepting H0.
Interestingly, the SPRT provably controls the type I error at
level α in this case. This follows, for example, by Ville’s
inequality which we will recap in Section II. In addition,
it is still guaranteed that the SPRT stops almost surely after
a ﬁnite number of samples if H1 is true [3], and therefore
is called conservative power-one SPRT, in particular studied
and espoused by Robbins [12]. A level-α sequential test of

d) Outline of the paper and our contributions: In this

paper, we propose a general sequential boosting method to
uniformly improve (super)martingale based sequential tests by
avoiding an overshoot at 1/α (Section II). This means that our
boosted sequential tests are never worse than the initial tests,
but may stop earlier and are more likely to achieve a rejection.
In Section III, we use this to uniformly improve conservative
power-one SPRTs for simple and one-sided nulls and alter-
natives. We provide nontrivial extensions and applications of
our method in Section IV, improving some existing conﬁdence

sequences, methods for sampling without replacement and
conformal martingales. In Section V, we demonstrate how our
boosting approach should be applied if a stop for futility is
to be included and type II error control is desired. Finally,
we discuss extensions of our method and existing approaches
for dealing with overshoot when using the SPRT (Section VI).
All formal proofs are provided in the supplementary material.
In Table I we compare Wald’s SPRTs with our boosted

versions. The type I error is denoted by α′ and the type II
error by β′. In the power-one case, our SPRT provides the
same guarantees as Wald’s SPRT, but uniformly improves
it in terms of sample size. For the two-sided case, Wald’s
conservative SPRT and our boosted SPRT provide valid type
I and type II error control while Wald’s approximate SPRT
does not. In addition, our two-sided SPRT outperformed
Wald’s approximate SPRT with respect to sample size in all
considered simulation scenarios and provably improves Wald’s
conservative SPRT.
e) Comparison to existing alternatives of Wald’s approx-

imated thresholds: We do not claim that our boosted tests are
optimal in the sense of (3). Hence, if the exact parameters
γ0 and γ1 for obtaining a desired type I and type II error
guarantee with the SPRT are known, one should employ the
usual SPRT with these thresholds. For example, this can be
the case in settings where the (asymptotic) approximations
by Siegmund [5] are reliable (see Section VI for a more
detailed discussion of this approach). However, we will see
that our approach can be applied in a much broader range of
settings, including in some nonparametric settings (like testing
exchangeability using conformal martingales), and provides
non-asymptotic control of the type I and type II error. Further
advantages over Siegmund’s and other approaches, such as the
use of numerical methods to determine the exact thresholds,
are discussed in Section VI-B.

B. Other Approaches to Avoid Wald’s Approximated
thresholds
The problem of “overshoot” in the SPRT was already noted

by Wald [1], [2] and examined in many previous works.
One line of work approximates the exact type I and type
II error of SPRTs based on Brownian motion and renewal
theory [5], [31], [32], [33]. This approach was particularly
driven by Siegmund, who gives a comprehensive overview in
his book [5]. The provided approximations are asymptotically
(for α →0 and β →0) correct under certain assumptions
including i.i.d. test statistics. Furthermore, using the Markov
property of the likelihood ratio in simple i.i.d. settings, one
can obtain the exact operating characteristics of the SPRT by
solving Fredholm integral equations (see, e.g., [34], [35], [36]).
In Figures 1 and 4, we compare our boosted SPRT to

the SPRT with Siegmund’s approximations in a simple i.i.d.
Gaussian testing setup H0 : Xt ∼N(0, 1) vs. H1 : Xt ∼

It is easy to see that Siegmund’s SPRT outperformed our

since due to the result by [4] (see (3)), the SPRT with

Therefore, if sufﬁciently accurate approximations of the exact
thresholds are available, e.g., if Siegmund’s theory applies or
the Fredholm integral equations hold, we recommend the use
of the SPRT with these thresholds. However, the advantage of
our proposed boosting technique is its much broader applica-

we do not make any separation or independence assumptions
and our method provides non-asymptotic as well as

To enable a more detailed and complete comparison of the

considered methods, Table IV displays some of the results in
comparison with Wald’s SPRTs and also shows the expected
sample size under the null distribution. To achieve higher
accuracy, these results were obtained using 100 000 simulation

Another approach is to truncate the SPRT by prespecifying a

maximum number of observations N. For simple distributions
of the likelihood ratio and sufﬁciently small N it is then possi-
ble to calculate the type I and type II error for given thresholds
exactly [37], which can be used to ﬁnd appropriate bounds for
the SPRT. Such an approach is frequently employed in group
sequential trials [38], [39]. For more complex distributions one
could approximate the error probabilities using simulations.
This often leads to considerable computational effort, which
sometimes can be reduced using importance sampling [21].
One limitation all the above approaches have in common

is that the test statistics and their distributions must be
speciﬁed in advance. This is not possible in the general
forecaster-skeptic testing protocol described in the previous
section. Hence, while our boosting approach is applicable
to such complex and adaptive testing protocols, all of the
aforementioned methods fail. Furthermore, after calculating
a boosting factor bt with our method, one can always plug
it back into the expectation ((12) in the one-sided or (28)
and (29) in the two-sided case) and only accept the boosting
factor if the expectation is indeed bounded by 1. If a boosting
factor cannot be accepted, one can try to calculate another
boosting factor or set bt = 1 if no greater boosting factor can
be found. In this way, one can always ensure that the resulting
test is conservative, meaning that it provides the desired type
I and type II error. This is neither possible with Siegmund’s
approach nor when using simulations.
Moreover, our approach provides a test supermartingale,

which yields an e-value at stopping times [17], [30], [40]. For
example, this can be important for optional continuation [30],
[40], combining the evidence with other test results [41] and
in multiple testing [42].
Due to its tight error control in non-i.i.d. sequential settings,

our boosted SPRT has the potential to become the state-of-the-
art method for a variety of applications.
For example, in clinical trials we often encounter testing
problems of the form H0 : θ∗≤0 vs. H1 : θ∗> 0, where θ∗

describes the treatment effect of a new treatment compared to
a control, and rigorous type I error control is required. Due to
the composite alternative, we usually need to estimate θ∗based
on the past data to apply the SPRT (see also Section III-B).
Therefore, the likelihood ratio becomes a product of non-i.i.d.

Furthermore, the extensions developed in Section IV offer
a range of promising applications. For example, martingale -

based conﬁdence sequences are used for A/B testing in tech
companies [43], [44], the sequential sampling without replace-
ment setting appears in risk-limiting election audits [25],
[45], [46] and conformal martingales can be used to verify
the i.i.d. assumption underlying many statistical and machine
learning methods [28], [47]. In all of those settings, improving
the employed sequential test by avoiding overshoot with our
boosting technique leads to faster and more efﬁcient decision-
making.
We introduced a general approach to uniformly improve

nonnegative (super)martingale based sequential tests by avoid-
ing an overshoot at the upper threshold 1/α (where α is
the desired type I error). We illustrated its application by
uniformly improving the conservative power-one SPRT for
one-sided null and alternative hypotheses. We also obtained an
alternative to the two-sided SPRT with Wald’s approximated
thresholds, where our alternative provides valid type I and
type II error control while often reducing the sample size.
Our sequential tests can also be used to tighten conﬁdence
sequences and apply in nontrivial settings like sampling with-
out replacement and conformal martingales.

d) Outline of the paper and our contributions: In this

paper, we propose a general sequential boosting method to
uniformly improve (super)martingale based sequential tests by
avoiding an overshoot at 1/α (Section II). This means that our
boosted sequential tests are never worse than the initial tests,
but may stop earlier and are more likely to achieve a rejection.
In Section III, we use this to uniformly improve conservative
power-one SPRTs for simple and one-sided nulls and alter-
natives. We provide nontrivial extensions and applications of
our method in Section IV, improving some existing conﬁdence

sequences, methods for sampling without replacement and
conformal martingales. In Section V, we demonstrate how our
boosting approach should be applied if a stop for futility is
to be included and type II error control is desired. Finally,
we discuss extensions of our method and existing approaches
for dealing with overshoot when using the SPRT (Section VI).
All formal proofs are provided in the supplementary material.
In Table I we compare Wald’s SPRTs with our boosted

versions. The type I error is denoted by α′ and the type II
error by β′. In the power-one case, our SPRT provides the
same guarantees as Wald’s SPRT, but uniformly improves
it in terms of sample size. For the two-sided case, Wald’s
conservative SPRT and our boosted SPRT provide valid type
I and type II error control while Wald’s approximate SPRT
does not. In addition, our two-sided SPRT outperformed
Wald’s approximate SPRT with respect to sample size in all
considered simulation scenarios and provably improves Wald’s
conservative SPRT.

imated thresholds: We do not claim that our boosted tests are
optimal in the sense of (3). Hence, if the exact parameters
γ0 and γ1 for obtaining a desired type I and type II error
guarantee with the SPRT are known, one should employ the
usual SPRT with these thresholds. For example, this can be
the case in settings where the (asymptotic) approximations
by Siegmund [5] are reliable (see Section VI for a more
detailed discussion of this approach). However, we will see
that our approach can be applied in a much broader range of
settings, including in some nonparametric settings (like testing
exchangeability using conformal martingales), and provides
non-asymptotic control of the type I and type II error. Further
advantages over Siegmund’s and other approaches, such as the
use of numerical methods to determine the exact thresholds,
are discussed in Section VI-B.

sections.heading: B. Other Approaches to Avoid Wald’s Approximated

items.text: The problem of “overshoot” in the SPRT was already noted

by Wald [1], [2] and examined in many previous works.
One line of work approximates the exact type I and type
II error of SPRTs based on Brownian motion and renewal
theory [5], [31], [32], [33]. This approach was particularly
driven by Siegmund, who gives a comprehensive overview in
his book [5]. The provided approximations are asymptotically
(for α →0 and β →0) correct under certain assumptions
including i.i.d. test statistics. Furthermore, using the Markov
property of the likelihood ratio in simple i.i.d. settings, one
can obtain the exact operating characteristics of the SPRT by
solving Fredholm integral equations (see, e.g., [34], [35], [36]).
In Figures 1 and 4, we compare our boosted SPRT to

the SPRT with Siegmund’s approximations in a simple i.i.d.
Gaussian testing setup H0 : Xt ∼N(0, 1) vs. H1 : Xt ∼
N(μ1, 1), where μ1 > 0 is the strength of the signal. Sieg-
mund’s approximations suggest to choose γ1 =
1−β

the SPRT with these approximated thresholds to our boosted
SPRT in the power-one (β = 0) case and in Figure 6 for
different desired type II errors β. In both cases α = 0.05 and
the implementation of our boosted SPRT is exactly the same
as in Figures 1 and 4. In this case we decided to use
Siegmund’s approximations for comparison, since they are
easier to apply than the integral equation approach and the
simulations showed that they are sufﬁciently accurate.
It is easy to see that Siegmund’s SPRT outperformed our

boosted SPRT in all considered cases. While the difference in
the power-one scenario is hardly visible, the gain in sample
size for larger β can be substantial. This is not surprising,
since due to the result by [4] (see (3)), the SPRT with
exact thresholds is optimal in terms of expected sample size.
Therefore, if sufﬁciently accurate approximations of the exact
thresholds are available, e.g., if Siegmund’s theory applies or
the Fredholm integral equations hold, we recommend the use
of the SPRT with these thresholds. However, the advantage of
our proposed boosting technique is its much broader applica-
bility. For example, the aforementioned approaches cannot be
applied to the one-sided SPRT without separation (Section III-
B) or any of the applications provided in Section IV, since the
employed test statistics are not independent (if (δt)t∈N and

(κt)t∈N are predictable in Sections S.1 and IV-C). In contrast,
we do not make any separation or independence assumptions
and our method provides non-asymptotic as well as

non-approximate error control. and our method provides
non-asymptotic as well as non-approximate error control.
To enable a more detailed and complete comparison of the

considered methods, Table IV displays some of the results in
comparison with Wald’s SPRTs and also shows the expected
sample size under the null distribution. To achieve higher
accuracy, these results were obtained using 100 000 simulation
runs.
Another approach is to truncate the SPRT by prespecifying a

maximum number of observations N. For simple distributions
of the likelihood ratio and sufﬁciently small N it is then possi-
ble to calculate the type I and type II error for given thresholds
exactly [37], which can be used to ﬁnd appropriate bounds for
the SPRT. Such an approach is frequently employed in group
sequential trials [38], [39]. For more complex distributions one
could approximate the error probabilities using simulations.
This often leads to considerable computational effort, which
sometimes can be reduced using importance sampling [21].
One limitation all the above approaches have in common

is that the test statistics and their distributions must be
speciﬁed in advance. This is not possible in the general
forecaster-skeptic testing protocol described in the previous
section. Hence, while our boosting approach is applicable
to such complex and adaptive testing protocols, all of the
aforementioned methods fail. Furthermore, after calculating
a boosting factor bt with our method, one can always plug
it back into the expectation ((12) in the one-sided or (28)
and (29) in the two-sided case) and only accept the boosting
factor if the expectation is indeed bounded by 1. If a boosting
factor cannot be accepted, one can try to calculate another
boosting factor or set bt = 1 if no greater boosting factor can
be found. In this way, one can always ensure that the resulting
test is conservative, meaning that it provides the desired type
I and type II error. This is neither possible with Siegmund’s
approach nor when using simulations.
Moreover, our approach provides a test supermartingale,

which yields an e-value at stopping times [17], [30], [40]. For
example, this can be important for optional continuation [30],
[40], combining the evidence with other test results [41] and
in multiple testing [42].
Due to its tight error control in non-i.i.d. sequential settings,

our boosted SPRT has the potential to become the state-of-the-
art method for a variety of applications.
For example, in clinical trials we often encounter testing
problems of the form H0 : θ∗≤0 vs. H1 : θ∗> 0, where θ∗

describes the treatment effect of a new treatment compared to
a control, and rigorous type I error control is required. Due to
the composite alternative, we usually need to estimate θ∗based
on the past data to apply the SPRT (see also Section III-B).
Therefore, the likelihood ratio becomes a product of non-i.i.d.
test statistics, which implies that all the alternative approaches
(Siegmund, Fredholm) mentioned in the previous section do

ethical (so that as few patients as possible are treated with
ineffective therapies), time-related (effective therapies should

be made available to the public as quickly as possible), and
economic reasons (recruiting trial participants can be very
expensive, especially for rare diseases).
Furthermore, the extensions developed in Section IV offer
a range of promising applications. For example, martingale -

based conﬁdence sequences are used for A/B testing in tech
companies [43], [44], the sequential sampling without replace-
ment setting appears in risk-limiting election audits [25],
[45], [46] and conformal martingales can be used to verify
the i.i.d. assumption underlying many statistical and machine
learning methods [28], [47]. In all of those settings, improving
the employed sequential test by avoiding overshoot with our
boosting technique leads to faster and more efﬁcient decision-
making.
We introduced a general approach to uniformly improve

nonnegative (super)martingale based sequential tests by avoid-
ing an overshoot at the upper threshold 1/α (where α is
the desired type I error). We illustrated its application by
uniformly improving the conservative power-one SPRT for
one-sided null and alternative hypotheses. We also obtained an
alternative to the two-sided SPRT with Wald’s approximated
thresholds, where our alternative provides valid type I and
type II error control while often reducing the sample size.
Our sequential tests can also be used to tighten conﬁdence
sequences and apply in nontrivial settings like sampling with-
out replacement and conformal martingales.

Probability Ratio Test by Avoiding Overshoot
Abstract— Wald’s sequential probability ratio test (SPRT) is

a cornerstone of sequential analysis. Based on desired type-I,
II error levels α, β, it stops when the likelihood ratio crosses
certain thresholds, guaranteeing optimality of the expected sam-
ple size. However, these thresholds are not closed form and the
test is often applied with approximate thresholds (1 −β)/α
and β/(1 −α) (approximate SPRT). When β
>
0, this

neither guarantees error control at α, β nor optimality. When
β = 0 (power-one SPRT), this method is conservative and not
optimal. The looseness in both cases is caused by overshoot:
the test statistic overshoots the thresholds at the stopping time.
Numerically calculating thresholds may be infeasible, and most
software packages do not do this. We improve the approximate
SPRT by modifying the test statistic to avoid overshoot. Our
‘sequential boosting’ technique uniformly improves power-one
SPRTs (β
=
0) for simple nulls and alternatives, or for

one-sided nulls and alternatives in exponential families. When
β > 0, our techniques provide guaranteed error control at α, β,
while needing less samples than the approximate SPRT in our
simulations. We also provide several nontrivial extensions: con-
ﬁdence sequences, sampling without replacement and conformal
martingales.

d) Outline of the paper and our contributions: In this

paper, we propose a general sequential boosting method to
uniformly improve (super)martingale based sequential tests by
avoiding an overshoot at 1/α (Section II). This means that our
boosted sequential tests are never worse than the initial tests,
but may stop earlier and are more likely to achieve a rejection.
In Section III, we use this to uniformly improve conservative
power-one SPRTs for simple and one-sided nulls and alter-
natives. We provide nontrivial extensions and applications of
our method in Section IV, improving some existing conﬁdence

sequences, methods for sampling without replacement and
conformal martingales. In Section V, we demonstrate how our
boosting approach should be applied if a stop for futility is
to be included and type II error control is desired. Finally,
we discuss extensions of our method and existing approaches
for dealing with overshoot when using the SPRT (Section VI).
All formal proofs are provided in the supplementary material.

advantages over Siegmund’s and other approaches, such as the

are discussed in Section VI-B.

is the likelihood ratio of θ0 to θ1 at time τ. With

this, we can estimate the type I error by the inverse of the

The boosting approach saves on average 3.4% to 11.8%

of the sample size compared to the SPRT in the considered
scenarios, while the percentage increases with the strength
of the signal. Furthermore, the boosted SPRT exhausts the
signiﬁcance level, while the SPRT is becoming increasingly
conservative for stronger signals. For all considered δ, the
mean computational time required for running one boosted
SPRT, including the numerical calculation of the correspond-
ing boosting factors, was below 0.05 seconds (performed on a

feasible in practice. In Supplementary Material S.2 we repeat

While the previous sections focused on power-one SPRTs

(β = 0) where we only stop to reject the null but not to accept
it, we now consider the case of β > 0, where we also wish
to stop if it is unlikely that we would reject the null if we
continued testing. We will show how we can use a boosting
technique similar to that in Section II to construct powerful
sequential tests that allow to “stop for futility” (stop and accept
the null).
Our main comparison point will be Wald’s approximate
two-sided SPRT, which uses thresholds of (1 −β)/α and

The problem of “overshoot” in the SPRT was already noted

by Wald [1], [2] and examined in many previous works.
One line of work approximates the exact type I and type
II error of SPRTs based on Brownian motion and renewal
theory [5], [31], [32], [33]. This approach was particularly
driven by Siegmund, who gives a comprehensive overview in
his book [5]. The provided approximations are asymptotically
(for α →0 and β →0) correct under certain assumptions
including i.i.d. test statistics. Furthermore, using the Markov
property of the likelihood ratio in simple i.i.d. settings, one
can obtain the exact operating characteristics of the SPRT by
solving Fredholm integral equations (see, e.g., [34], [35], [36]).
In Figures 1 and 4, we compare our boosted SPRT to

Gaussian testing setup H0 : Xt ∼N(0, 1) vs. H1 : Xt ∼

It is easy to see that Siegmund’s SPRT outperformed our

boosted SPRT in all considered cases. While the difference in
the power-one scenario is hardly visible, the gain in sample
size for larger β can be substantial. This is not surprising,
since due to the result by [4] (see (3)), the SPRT with
exact thresholds is optimal in terms of expected sample size.
Therefore, if sufﬁciently accurate approximations of the exact
thresholds are available, e.g., if Siegmund’s theory applies or
the Fredholm integral equations hold, we recommend the use
of the SPRT with these thresholds. However, the advantage of
our proposed boosting technique is its much broader applica-

and our method provides non-asymptotic as well as

To enable a more detailed and complete comparison of the

considered methods, Table IV displays some of the results in
comparison with Wald’s SPRTs and also shows the expected
sample size under the null distribution. To achieve higher
accuracy, these results were obtained using 100 000 simulation

Another approach is to truncate the SPRT by prespecifying a

maximum number of observations N. For simple distributions
of the likelihood ratio and sufﬁciently small N it is then possi-
ble to calculate the type I and type II error for given thresholds
exactly [37], which can be used to ﬁnd appropriate bounds for
the SPRT. Such an approach is frequently employed in group
sequential trials [38], [39]. For more complex distributions one
could approximate the error probabilities using simulations.
This often leads to considerable computational effort, which
sometimes can be reduced using importance sampling [21].
One limitation all the above approaches have in common

is that the test statistics and their distributions must be
speciﬁed in advance. This is not possible in the general
forecaster-skeptic testing protocol described in the previous
section. Hence, while our boosting approach is applicable
to such complex and adaptive testing protocols, all of the
aforementioned methods fail. Furthermore, after calculating
a boosting factor bt with our method, one can always plug
it back into the expectation ((12) in the one-sided or (28)
and (29) in the two-sided case) and only accept the boosting
factor if the expectation is indeed bounded by 1. If a boosting
factor cannot be accepted, one can try to calculate another
boosting factor or set bt = 1 if no greater boosting factor can
be found. In this way, one can always ensure that the resulting
test is conservative, meaning that it provides the desired type
I and type II error. This is neither possible with Siegmund’s
approach nor when using simulations.
Moreover, our approach provides a test supermartingale,

which yields an e-value at stopping times [17], [30], [40]. For
example, this can be important for optional continuation [30],
[40], combining the evidence with other test results [41] and
in multiple testing [42].
Due to its tight error control in non-i.i.d. sequential settings,

our boosted SPRT has the potential to become the state-of-the-
art method for a variety of applications.
For example, in clinical trials we often encounter testing
problems of the form H0 : θ∗≤0 vs. H1 : θ∗> 0, where θ∗

describes the treatment effect of a new treatment compared to
a control, and rigorous type I error control is required. Due to
the composite alternative, we usually need to estimate θ∗based
on the past data to apply the SPRT (see also Section III-B).
Therefore, the likelihood ratio becomes a product of non-i.i.d.
test statistics, which implies that all the alternative approaches

boosted SPRT is the most efﬁcient sequential test for this
testing problem. In clinical trials, efﬁciency is essential for
ethical (so that as few patients as possible are treated with
ineffective therapies), time-related (effective therapies should

be made available to the public as quickly as possible), and
economic reasons (recruiting trial participants can be very
expensive, especially for rare diseases).
Furthermore, the extensions developed in Section IV offer
a range of promising applications. For example, martingale -

based conﬁdence sequences are used for A/B testing in tech
companies [43], [44], the sequential sampling without replace-
ment setting appears in risk-limiting election audits [25],
[45], [46] and conformal martingales can be used to verify
the i.i.d. assumption underlying many statistical and machine
learning methods [28], [47]. In all of those settings, improving
the employed sequential test by avoiding overshoot with our
boosting technique leads to faster and more efﬁcient decision-
making.
We introduced a general approach to uniformly improve

nonnegative (super)martingale based sequential tests by avoid-
ing an overshoot at the upper threshold 1/α (where α is
the desired type I error). We illustrated its application by
uniformly improving the conservative power-one SPRT for
one-sided null and alternative hypotheses. We also obtained an
alternative to the two-sided SPRT with Wald’s approximated
thresholds, where our alternative provides valid type I and
type II error control while often reducing the sample size.
Our sequential tests can also be used to tighten conﬁdence
sequences and apply in nontrivial settings like sampling with-
out replacement and conformal martingales.

Lasse Fischer received the B.Sc., M.Sc., and the Ph.D. degrees in mathe-
matics from the University of Bremen, Bremen, Germany, in 2019, 2022, and
2025, respectively. From 2022 to 2025, he was a Research Assistant with the
University of Bremen. During this time, he spent four months on a research
visit with Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, USA. He is currently a
Post-Doctoral Researcher with the University of Bremen. His main research
interests include (online) multiple testing, anytime-valid sequential inference,
and post-hoc decision-making.

Aaditya Ramdas received the Ph.D. degree in statistics and machine learning
in 2015. He is currently a tenured Associate Professor with the Department of
Statistics and Data Science and the Machine Learning Department, Carnegie
Mellon University. He works on mathematical statistics and learning. He is
best known for his work on e-values, conﬁdence sequences, multiple testing,
and conformal prediction. He is a fellow of IMS. He received the Bernoulli
New Researcher Award, the NSF CAREER Award, the IIT Bombay Young
Alumnus Achievement Award, and the Sloan Fellowship. He was the Program
Chair of AISTATS.

Comparison to existing alternatives of Wald’s approximated thresholds: We do not claim that our boosted tests are optimal in the sense of (3). Hence, if the exact parameters \gamma0 and \gamma1 for obtaining a desired type I and type II error guarantee with the SPRT are known, one should employ the usual SPRT with these thresholds. For example, this can be the case in settings where the (asymptotic) approximations by Siegmund [5] are reliable (see Section VI for a more detailed discussion of this approach). However, we will see that our approach can be applied in a much broader range of settings, including in some nonparametric settings (like testing exchangeability using conformal martingales), and provides non-asymptotic control of the type I and type II error. Further advantages over Siegmund’s and other approaches, such as the use of numerical methods to determine the exact thresholds, are discussed in Section VI-B.

We now demonstrate some nontrivial extensions and applications of our boosting method. First, we show how it can be used for tighten conﬁdence sequences in Section IV-A. Then, we exemplify its use in sampling without replacement situations (Section IV-B) and with conformal martingales (Section IV-C) for testing the assumption of i.i.d. data.
SPRT While the previous sections focused on power-one SPRTs (
= 0) where we only stop to reject the null but not to accept it, we now consider the case of

> 0, where we also wish to stop if it is unlikely that we would reject the null if we continued testing. We will show how we can use a boosting technique similar to that in Section II to construct powerful sequential tests that allow to “stop for futility” (stop and accept the null).

In this section, we will ﬁrst develop a general method with valid type I error control for test supermartingales, and then show how the stop for futility can be chosen to obtain tight type I and type II error control in the SPRT case. The latter method often outperforms Wald’s approximate SPRT in the sense that while guaranteeing (a) and (b), our method also manages to typically/often stop sooner than Wald’s (though not guaranteeing (c)).

One line of work approximates the exact type I and type II error of SPRTs based on Brownian motion and renewal theory [5], [31], [32], [33]. This approach was particularly driven by Siegmund, who gives a comprehensive overview in his book [5]. The provided approximations are asymptotically (for

→0) correct under certain assumptions including i.i.d. test statistics. Furthermore, using the Markov property of the likelihood ratio in simple i.i.d. settings, one can obtain the exact operating characteristics of the SPRT by solving Fredholm integral equations (see, e.g., [34], [35], [36]).

Therefore, if sufﬁciently accurate approximations of the exact thresholds are available, e.g., if Siegmund’s theory applies or the Fredholm integral equations hold, we recommend the use of the SPRT with these thresholds. To enable a more detailed and complete comparison of theconsidered methods, Table IV displays some of the results in comparison with Wald’s SPRTs and also shows the expected sample size under the null distribution. To achieve higher accuracy, these results were obtained using 100 000 simulation runs.

Another approach is to truncate the SPRT by prespecifying amaximum number of observations N. For simple distributions of the likelihood ratio and sufﬁciently small N it is then possible to calculate the type I and type II error for given thresholds exactly [37], which can be used to ﬁnd appropriate bounds for the SPRT. Such an approach is frequently employed in group sequential trials [38], [39]. For more complex distributions one could approximate the error probabilities using simulations. This often leads to considerable computational effort, which sometimes can be reduced using importance sampling [21].

One limitation all the above approaches have in commonis that the test statistics and their distributions must be speciﬁed in advance. This is not possible in the general forecaster-skeptic testing protocol described in the previous section. Hence, while our boosting approach is applicable to such complex and adaptive testing protocols, all of the aforementioned methods fail. Furthermore, after calculating a boosting factor bt with our method, one can always plug it back into the expectation ((12) in the one-sided or (28) and (29) in the two-sided case) and only accept the boosting factor if the expectation is indeed bounded by 1. If a boosting factor cannot be accepted, one can try to calculate another boosting factor or set bt = 1 if no greater boosting factor can be found. In this way, one can always ensure that the resulting test is conservative, meaning that it provides the desired type I and type II error. This is neither possible with Siegmund’s approach nor when using simulations.

Moreover, our approach provides a test supermartingale, which yields an e-value at stopping times [17], [30], [40]. For example, this can be important for optional continuation [30], [40], combining the evidence with other test results [41] and in multiple testing [42].

Lasse Fischer received the B.Sc., M.Sc., and the Ph.D. degrees in mathematics from the University of Bremen, Bremen, Germany, in 2019, 2022, and 2025, respectively. From 2022 to 2025, he was a Research Assistant with the University of Bremen. During this time, he spent four months on a research visit with Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, USA. He is currently a Post-Doctoral Researcher with the University of Bremen. His main research interests include (online) multiple testing, anytime-valid sequential inference, and post-hoc decision-making.

Aaditya Ramdas received the Ph.D. degree in statistics and machine learning in 2015. He is currently a tenured Associate Professor with the Department of Statistics and Data Science and the Machine Learning Department, Carnegie Mellon University. He works on mathematical statistics and learning. He is best known for his work on e-values, conﬁdence sequences, multiple testing, and conformal prediction. He is a fellow of IMS. He received the Bernoulli New Researcher Award, the NSF CAREER Award, the IIT Bombay Young Alumnus Achievement Award, and the Sloan Fellowship. He was the Program Chair of AISTATS.
